claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is primarily governed by synergy between configurational entropy and grain-boundary density.
High configurational entropy reduces the driving force for elemental segregation.
A high density of nanoscale grain boundaries accelerates atomic diffusion.
A high density of nanoscale grain boundaries accelerates oxidation.
Changing grain-boundary density provides direct control over high-temperature stability.
Rapid mixing produces a nanocrystalline high-entropy nanoalloy with a high grain-boundary density.
The as-synthesized alloy has a uniform compositional distribution.
Post-synthesis annealing increases grain size and reduces grain-boundary density.
The annealing treatment can reduce grain-boundary density without significantly changing alloy composition.
Grain boundaries provide fast paths for oxygen ingress.
Grain boundaries provide fast paths for elemental interdiffusion.
Reducing grain-boundary density slows oxygen ingress and elemental interdiffusion.
At approximately 1000°C in air, the annealed sample will oxidize more slowly than the as-synthesized nanocrystalline baseline.
The annealed sample will form a more uniform oxide layer than the baseline.
The annealed sample will form a thinner oxide layer than the baseline.
The annealed sample will exhibit less phase separation than the baseline during high-temperature exposure.
The annealed sample will exhibit less elemental segregation than the baseline during high-temperature exposure.
The prediction may not apply in inert environments and may vary across alloy compositions and high-entropy-alloy systems.
